question: After staging the reservation form (click "Stage request") and then committing it (click "Commit booking"), the page prints an object to the browser console under action calendar.reserve. Locate the anchor function for the request_body field of that object. The same request_body value is also used as the body of the fetch request that is sent (POST /api/calendar/reserve). The anchor is the first target-specific request-body construction function on the dynamic behavior chain: it sits after routing, click-time runtime collection, form-state collection and input preparation, and its own body rewrites the reservation form fields (date, time, service) into the target observable request body - rather than merely collecting inputs, dispatching control, packaging a return value, or emitting it to the console sink or fetch call. Return exactly one complete function together with its code location; do not return a generic utility, an event handler, the whole call chain, or the final sink. Note: you can only inspect the code under captures; you cannot access the full source repository.

response_schema.function_name: The function identifier exactly as it appears at the head of the function in the captures bundle (the obfuscated name may be a mangled token such as _0xabc123). Do not invent a source-level name.
response_schema.file: Path to the captures .js file that contains the function, e.g. captures/devtools-source-dump/127.0.0.1_4193/assets/calendar.app.bundle.js

slice.start_line: integer, 1-based line where the function starts in that file
slice.end_line: integer, 1-based line where the function ends
slice.start_offset: integer, 0-based byte offset of the first character of the function
slice.end_offset: integer, 0-based byte offset one past the last character of the function (exclusive)
slice.code: The complete function source text, from the function keyword through its matching closing brace

public_constraints: Only code visible under captures is in scope.
Return a single JSON object that matches answer_format.response_schema (one top-1 function), not a list of candidate chains.
function_name must be the identifier as it appears in captures; slice.code must be one complete function (balanced braces), not a signature fragment or a partial body.
Do not return the final console sink or the fetch call site.
Do not return a generic DOM reader, normalizer or dispatcher when a more target-specific request-body constructor is present.
Constrain the observable by both action and field.
The page contains many high-similarity reservation encoder configurations; only the encoder selected by the live commit route constructs the observed request body.
anchor_definition_general: A function is target-specific (with respect to the observable above) if at least one statement in its body constructs or binds the target value, writes the target field, or dispatches the target action, and removing that statement would break the observed output under the prescribed interaction. A function is generic if it is a reusable utility (hash/encode/serialize/normalize/collect-features), a control-flow dispatcher (router/interceptor-pipeline/event-bus/scheduler), or a preparation routine (validate input/collect UI state/lifecycle hook) whose body would look the same regardless of which behavior it currently serves. The anchor is the unique target-specific function on the chain whose immediate caller is generic, i.e. the shallowest target-specific function on the path from the trigger to the sink. If a target-specific function C is called by a generic dispatcher B and itself calls a generic utility D (e.g. a hash routine), the anchor is C, not B and not D. If a generic function A merely writes whatever its callee B returns into the target field, and B is dedicated to computing that value, the anchor is B. If the target-specific statement is one branch inside a larger function F that also handles unrelated cases, F is still a valid anchor candidate.
anchor_worked_example: Worked example (different scenario, illustration only): a checkout page emits body.order_sig_v2 after the user clicks Submit Order. The chain is: click Submit Order -> construct order draft (generic prep) -> encode checkout state (generic prep) -> collect async profile receipt (generic prep) -> compose request envelope (generic prep) -> run interceptor pipeline (generic dispatcher) -> select sealing interceptor (ANCHOR) -> canonicalize payload fields (nested helper) -> fold payload with receipt and pepper (nested helper) -> compute digest (generic SHA-256 core utility) -> write body.order_sig_v2 -> send request (generic wrapper/sink). The sealing interceptor is the anchor: its immediate caller is the generic interceptor-pipeline dispatcher, and its own body is the highest point on the chain whose code, read alone, explains why order_sig_v2 specifically is produced. Functions below it (canonicalize, fold) are nested helpers; the digest routine is a core utility; dispatcher and sender are path/wrapper. Other same-click values such as analytics_sig or coupon_digest are off-chain decoys. Apply the same reasoning to the actual page and bundle.
